sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Unified multimodal generation covers discrete, continuous, and hybrid paradigms. Discrete approaches with single-codebook visual tokenizers align naturally with text modeling but have limited representational capacity. Continuous and hybrid approaches retain richer visual representations, but they model text and images in heterogeneous spaces with different training objectives, potentially introducing optimization conflicts between modalities with misaligned representation spaces. These choices expose a central question: how to efficiently model high-capacity visual representations alongside textual content in a shared optimization space within a single backbone. We present Intern Lumina U2, to our knowledge the first diffusion language model to represent multi-codebook visual tokens in a fully discrete space. Each visual position is represented by a group of codes from complementary codebooks, increasing its representational capacity while preserving compatibility with discrete text modeling. At the input, the embeddings are concatenated at each position; at the output, a lightweight multi-codebook autoregressive head predicts the codes within each position sequentially, while the diffusion backbone processes all positions in parallel. Built on the unified 4D representation of AToken, Intern Lumina U2 supports image, video, and 3D inputs within a single backbone and achieves leading performance among unified models in visual understanding, image generation, and image editing. We further build a full-stack training, inference, and evaluation system on both Ascend and NVIDIA platforms to verify the cross-platform effectiveness of our model. We also improve the inference efficiency through a stability-aware sampling strategy, which combines confidence-plateau-guided unmasking approach with drift-triggered cache refreshing mechanisms, accelerating image generation by 4.45x.

Intern Lumina U2: Multi-Codebook Diffusion Large Language Model for Omni-Visual Understanding and Image Generation 1. Introduction Unified multimodal models integrate visual understanding and generation within single model (Chameleon Team, 2024; Deng et al., 2025; Tian et al., 2026). However, architectural sharing alone does not constitute complete unification, since understanding and generation may still rely on separate representations and training objectives (Qiu et al., 2026). To go beyond architectural unification, we identify two principles for unifying understanding and generation more comprehensively. First, text and visual content should be mapped into shared optimization space under single objective. Although hybrid designs (Deng et al., 2025; Fan et al., 2025; Tian et al., 2026) can achieve high visual fidelity by retaining continuous visual states and delegating synthesis to continuous decoder, they optimize visual generation with continuous objective distinct from the text objective and often adopt separate visual encoders for understanding and generation, leading to optimization difficulties. Second, the generation process should respect the intrinsic structure of each modality. Text follows natural sequential order, whereas visual content has no canonical generation order: each region depends on both its local neighborhood and long-range global context. The generation process should therefore decode text sequentially while refining visual content in parallel with bidirectional context. Discrete masked diffusion provides natural basis for satisfying the requirements above. It applies masked-prediction objective to discrete text and visual tokens, thereby optimizing both modalities within common discrete space. Under this formulation, each task is specified by partitioning the token sequence into observed conditioning tokens and masked prediction targets. Understanding and generation are thereby cast as distinct conditional queries to the same model, rather than as separate tasks with task-specific objectives. Moreover, masked diffusion decodes tokens in parallel through iterative refinement without imposing fixed generation order (Nie et al., 2025; Chang et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2025; Xin et al., 2025), allowing each spatial position to be refined with bidirectional access to both local and global context. However, existing discrete unified models (Xin et al., 2025; Xie et al., 2025a; Yang et al., 2025) remain limited in visual representation capacity, as single-codebook tokenization compresses the visual information at each position into single discrete code. Such compact representation is insufficient both for faithful reconstruction and for covering the full range of visual tasks (Ma et al., 2025a). This motivates us to design unified discrete framework that carries high-capacity visual representation in shared space under single training objective, while modeling it efficiently with unified backbone. To this end, we present Intern Lumina U2, to our knowledge the first diffusion language model that models multi-codebook visual states in fully discrete space, with AToken (Lu et al., 2026) as the visual tokenizer and LLaDA2.0 (Bie et al., 2025) as the backbone. Intern Lumina U2 encodes images, videos, and 3D assets into unified 4D code space and organizes these visual tokens together with text tokens in unified packed-sequence format, so that understanding and generation across all these modalities are formulated over the same sequence representation and handled by shared backbone. Each visual position carries complementary codes: independent embedding tables concatenated at the input preserve codebook identity for efficient training, while lightweight multi-codebook autoregressive head models the dependencies among the codes within each position. Within this shared representation, multi-task masking mechanism assigns each task its own masking scheme, so that understanding, generation, and editing across modalities are trained jointly under single objective. For image generation, stability-aware inference strategy commits tokens at confidence plateaus and refreshes the cache on hidden-state drift, achieving 4.45 end-to-end speedup. We further build the operators, parallelization strategies, and system adaptations for training, inference, and evaluation on 1,024 Ascend 910B NPUs, with smaller-scale NVIDIA reference run using the same architecture and optimization recipe but smaller training budget for cross-platform validation. 3 Intern Lumina U2: Multi-Codebook Diffusion Large Language Model for Omni-Visual Understanding and Image Generation Extensive experiments on image, video, and 3D understanding, as well as image generation and editing, demonstrate the effectiveness of this unified design. To our knowledge, Intern Lumina U2 is the first diffusion language model to support this full combination of visual modalities and capabilities. Trained on data curated by unified pipeline that organizes heterogeneous sources under common protocol, the model achieves leading performance among unified multimodal models across our evaluations. With only 1.4B activated parameters, it ranks first on six of ten image-understanding benchmarks and improves on eight of ten over the same-backbone LLaDA2.0-Uni (Bie et al., 2026). It also shows superior performance on all three video benchmarks (Fu et al., 2025b; Zhou et al., 2025b; Li et al., 2024) and on 3D MM-Vet (Qi et al., 2024), and among unified models it delivers strong text-to-image generation on DPG-Bench (Hu et al., 2024), UniGenBench (Wang et al., 2025b), TIIF-Bench (Wei et al., 2026), and GenEval (Ghosh et al., 2023). It also performs strongly on physicsfaithful scientific-diagram generation. These results establish Intern Lumina U2 as competitive unified discrete foundation model for omni-visual understanding and generation. Contributions. Multi-codebook discrete modeling for unified dLLMs. To our knowledge, Intern Lumina U2 is the first unified diffusion language model built on multi-codebook visual states, with visual prediction factorized across spatial positions and codebooks. Omni-visual understanding in unified discrete space. Intern Lumina U2 is the first diffusion language model to unify visual understanding across images, videos, and 3D assets with image generation and editing, moving unified multimodal modeling toward general omni-visual paradigm. Full-stack adaptation and validation on Ascend. We complete the full-stack adaptation of Intern Lumina U2 on 1,024 Ascend 910B NPUs, enabling end-to-end training, inference, and comprehensive evaluation on the platform. Efficient image-generation inference. We introduce Plateau-Halton sampling with V-verify (PHV), which commits tokens at confidence plateaus and refreshes the cache on hidden-state drift, achieving 4.45 speedup in end-to-end image-generation latency with favorable qualityefficiency trade-off. Broad empirical validation. Intern Lumina U2 achieves leading performance across image, video, and 3D understanding, text-to-image generation, image editing, and scientific-diagram generation, demonstrating the effectiveness and breadth of the proposed unified framework. 2. Related Work We relate Intern Lumina U2 to four bodies of work: unified multimodal models, diffusion language models, multi-codebook visual representations, and inference acceleration for masked diffusion. Table 1 groups representative systems by backbone paradigm and summarizes their capability and design profile; Intern Lumina U2 is the only system in the comparison that combines image generation, perception across images, videos, and 3D assets, and masked-diffusion decoding over multicodebook visual state. It represents all three visual input modalities with discrete backbone tokens and generates images without separate continuous diffusion or flow generator. Unified multimodal understanding and generation. One line of work models image generation as discrete visual-token prediction within the backbone. Chameleon and Emu3 use shared vocabulary for text and visual codes under next-token prediction (Chameleon Team, 2024; Wang et al., 2026a), whereas MMaDA and Lumina-DiMOO use masked prediction for both modalities (Yang et al., 2025; 4 Intern Lumina U2: Multi-Codebook Diffusion Large Language Model for Omni-Visual Understanding and Image Generation Xin et al., 2025). Related discrete-generation designs include Janus and Janus-Pro, which decouple the understanding encoder from the generation tokenizer (Wu et al., 2025b; Chen et al., 2025); VAR and OneCAT, which use coarse-to-fine next-scale prediction (Tian et al., 2024; Li et al., 2026a); and Emu3.5, which converts next-token image decoding to bidirectional parallel prediction for faster inference (Cui et al., 2025). second line models image generation in continuous space with diffusion or flow objective. Transfusion combines text next-token loss with image diffusion in one Transformer (Zhou et al., 2025a), UniFluid models each position with diffusion head (Fan et al., 2025), BAGEL and InternVL-U use ViT features for understanding and VAE-space flow matching for generation (Deng et al., 2025; Tian et al., 2026), and SenseNova-U1 moves flow matching to pixel space (SenseNova Team, 2026). third, hybrid route predicts discrete semantic visual tokens in the backbone and reconstructs images with separate continuous generator. LLaDA2.0-Uni follows this design: its backbone models text and visual tokens under shared masked-prediction objective, while diffusion decoder synthesizes images conditioned on the predicted visual tokens (Bie et al., 2026). Single-codebook discrete representations constrain the detail and semantics carried at each visual position. Continuous and hybrid designs support richer image synthesis, but retain continuous generative objective distinct from text-token classification, either within the backbone or in separate generator. Intern Lumina U2 instead uses multi-codebook discrete representations for image, video, and 3D inputs, while training text prediction and image generation under shared objective. Diffusion language models. LLaDA showed that masked diffusion language models trained from scratch can match strong AR baselines, replacing left-to-right decoding with parallel iterative recovery (Nie et al., 2025), and LLaDA2.0 converts pretrained AR Mixture-of-Experts model into blockwise diffusion LM, preserving its knowledge while enabling parallel decoding (Bie et al., 2025). This family has been extended to vision in several ways: LLaDA-V feeds features from vision encoder into the diffusion LM for understanding (You et al., 2026a), and LLaDA-o pairs discrete masked diffusion for text with continuous diffusion for images (You et al., 2026b). Among the unified models discussed above, MMaDA and Lumina-DiMOO extend masked prediction to both text and image tokens (Yang et al., 2025; Xin et al., 2025), while LLaDA2.0-Uni adopts the converted LLaDA2.0 backbone with block-wise masked prediction (Bie et al., 2026). Intern Lumina U2 also starts from LLaDA2.0-mini and extends this family along two axes: the visual state becomes multi-codebook visual token, and the same model covers image, video, and 3D inputs. Multi-codebook representations and depth decoding. Residual and factorized quantization raise the capacity of discrete visual states without lengthening the spatial grid: RQ-Transformer decodes residual codes with spatial-plus-depth Transformer (Lee et al., 2022), VILA-U brings multi-codebook depth decoding into an AR unified model (Wu et al., 2025d), UniTok folds HW codes into HW backbone positions (Ma et al., 2025a), and TokenBridge documents the dependence that is lost when the codes of one position are predicted independently (Wang et al., 2025c). AToken supplies the shared image/video/3D multi-codebook representation used here (Lu et al., 2026). These works establish multi-codebook modeling in autoregressive systems. Intern Lumina U2 instead makes the multi-codebook visual token the visual state of masked-diffusion language model: the backbone refines spatial positions in parallel, while the multi-codebook AR head models the dependence among codes within each position (Section 3.4). This factorization keeps the backbone sequence length independent of without treating the codebooks as conditionally independent. Accelerating masked-diffusion decoding. Acceleration methods for masked generation follow two routes. Because visual-token confidence sits far below the absolute thresholds of Fast-dLLM-style commit rules (Section 6.2.2), it adapts both the commit schedule and the cache refresh from temporal signals, confidence plateaus and measured hidden-state drift (Section 6.2). 3. Model Architecture 3.1. Overview As shown in Figure 3, Intern Lumina U2 is masked diffusion language model that supports visual understanding over images, videos, and 3D assets, as well as image generation and editing within unified model (Figure 3). To model all tasks with single backbone and shared training objective, we represent every modality as discrete tokens. Specifically, visual inputs (images, videos, and 3D assets) are first converted into visual tokens by frozen visual tokenizer, AToken (Section 3.2), while 6 Intern Lumina U2: Multi-Codebook Diffusion Large Language Model for Omni-Visual Understanding and Image Generation Figure 3: Overall architecture of Intern Lumina U2. Visual inputs are encoded into visual tokens by AToken and text into text tokens; the MoE diffusion LLM recovers masked text tokens through the text head, with text answers generated by block diffusion, and masked visual tokens through the multi-codebook AR head, which predicts the codes of each visual token sequentially. text is converted into text tokens by the native tokenizer of the base language model, LLaDA2.0-mini. The resulting visual and text tokens, together with the target tokens (either text answer or target image, represented as the mask tokens), are arranged into single sequence. The MoE diffusion LLM (Section 3.3) processes this sequence and predicts the masked tokens in modality-specific manner. Masked text tokens are predicted by text head and generated block by block. In contrast, masked visual tokens are predicted by multi-codebook AR head (Section 3.4): each visual token contains K=8 discrete codes, and the head predicts visual tokens at different positions in parallel while generating the discrete codes within each token sequentially. Finally, the AToken decoder maps the predicted visual codes back to pixels. 3.2. Unified Visual Tokenizer The visual tokenizer serves as the interface between raw visual data (images, videos, and 3D assets) and the model, and therefore constrains both generation and understanding. As discussed in the previous section, Intern Lumina U2 places two requirements on its visual tokenizer: (1) it must produce discrete visual tokens that can be modeled in the same way as text tokens, so that all tasks can share single masked-diffusion objective; and (2) these tokens must preserve both the low-level detail for generation and the high-level semantics needed for understanding. However, existing tokenizers are typically specialized for either low-level detail or high-level semantics. For example, tokenizers 7 Intern Lumina U2: Multi-Codebook Diffusion Large Language Model for Omni-Visual Understanding and Image Generation trained for reconstruction, such as VQGAN (Esser et al., 2021), keep fine detail but are not trained to align with language, whereas semantic encoders such as SigLIP (Zhai et al., 2023) align well with text but are not trained to reconstruct pixels. We therefore adopt AToken (Lu et al., 2026) as the visual tokenizer. AToken is initialized from pretrained SigLIP2 encoder (Tschannen et al., 2025) and trained jointly for reconstruction and understanding. As result, its tokens carry semantic structure while still supporting faithful reconstruction. In addition, AToken encodes images, videos, and 3D assets into shared 4D latent space, so that single tokenizer serves all three modalities. We use its discrete configuration, which quantizes each location of the latent grid with finite scalar quantization (FSQ) (Mentzer et al., 2024) over K=8 codebooks. Each codebook is vocabulary of 4096 entries, and code is the index of one entry, so each location is represented by codes = (c1, . . . , cK), one per codebook. We call such location visual position and its codes visual token (Figure 3). Compared with single code per position, the eight codes give the representation more capacity for fine visual detail. The tokenizer is kept frozen during training, and the grid shapes, flattening orders, and structural tokens are listed in Appendix B. 3.3. Backbone We build our backbone upon LLaDA2.0-mini (Bie et al., 2025), masked diffusion language model obtained by converting pretrained autoregressive mixture-of-experts (MoE) language model (Ling Team, 2025) into block diffusion model. It has 16B parameters in total, of which 1.4B are activated per token. Among its 20 Transformer layers, the first employs dense feed-forward network, while the remaining 19 are MoE layers. Each MoE layer consists of 256 routed experts and single shared expert, with 8 routed experts activated per token. LLaDA2.0-mini is language model which generates text via block diffusion: sequence is divided into blocks of consecutive tokens, and each block is denoised by masked diffusion conditioned on all preceding blocks. Accordingly, it generates text block by block at inference: the masked tokens within the current block are predicted in parallel and iteratively refined over several denoising steps, while the keyvalue cache of previously completed blocks is reused. Since LLaDA2.0-mini already performs masked diffusion over text, we can directly inherit its language capabilities without an additional autoregressive-to-diffusion conversion (Gong et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2025a; Bie et al., 2025). We introduce two modifications to LLaDA2.0-mini while keeping all other components unchanged, including the Transformer layers, the text embedding table, the text head, and the <mask> token. First, we add the visual input and output interfaces described in Section 3.4, which account for 0.65B parameters. Second, we replace the attention mask with our proposed task-aware attention mask. LLaDA2.0-mini was trained exclusively on text with block-wise attention mask, whereas our Intern Lumina U2 also contains visual conditions and visual answers. We therefore design task-aware attention mask that controls attention among these segments according to the task (Section 3.5). It is worthy to mention that we retain the native positional encoding (e.g. 1D RoPE (Su et al., 2024)) of the backbone for visual tokens, rather than introducing dedicated 2D or 3D scheme, which preserves the positional prior learned in pretraining. Since 1D RoPE does not explicitly encode spatial structure, the spatial or spatio-temporal layout of each visual input is instead indicated by structural delimiter tokens inserted into the sequence (Appendix B). In this way, images, videos, and 3D assets are all represented in the same 1D token sequence as text. 3.4. Multi-Codebook Input and Output With multi-codebook tokenizer, each visual position is represented by codes, all of which must be encoded at the input and predicted at the output. We compare three designs for handling the 8 Intern Lumina U2: Multi-Codebook Diffusion Large Language Model for Omni-Visual Understanding and Image Generation codes of visual token. The first flattens them into separate tokens, which multiplies the sequence length by K. The second keeps one backbone token per visual position but predicts the codes independently, which ignores the dependence among them. The third keeps one backbone token per visual position and models the codes jointly. Our Intern Lumina U2 adopts the third design: at the input, the codes of each visual position are merged into single backbone token, and at the output, they are predicted jointly by the multi-codebook AR head. Unified Data Format with Data Packing Having specified the representation of single visual position, we now describe the organization of complete samples into training sequences. All tasks, from text-only dialogue to image generation and editing, share unified packed sequence format. Moreover, to determine the attention mask and calculate loss, each token in this format is annotated with five metadata fields: type (text condition, visual condition, structural token, text answer, or visual answer), turn index, noise state (clean or noisy), block index, and position ID. Dialogue structure and sequence layout. Every sample is first formatted as dialogue between user and an assistant, in which each turn consists of user message and the assistants reply to it. 10 Intern Lumina U2: Multi-Codebook Diffusion Large Language Model for Omni-Visual Understanding and Image Generation Figure 5: Training and inference of the multi-codebook AR head: one teacher-forced causal pass yields all logits at training; at inference the prefix grows for steps, each sampled code ˆck is embedded into ek and appended. Positions are processed in parallel, codebooks autoregressively. The conditions, provided by the user, consist of text prompt, an image, video, 3D asset, or any combination of them. The answers, provided by the assistant, are partly masked during training and serve as the prediction targets. Text answers and visual answers follow different layouts, which we describe in the following. Text answers. text answer consists of <BOA>, the answer tokens, and <EOA>, and its final block is padded to multiple of the block length with additional <EOA> tokens before corruption. End-of-answer padding thus becomes an ordinary supervised target, and every block contains exactly maskable tokens. When sample is packed into sequence, its conditions and noisy answers are placed in dialogue order, followed by clean copy of each text answer: [ clean context + noisy answer } {z dialogue stream clean copy } {z clean stream ]. The clean copies serve as unmasked context for later blocks and turns. In multi-turn understanding, for example, later turns condition on earlier text answers by attending to their clean copies (Figure 6d). The clean copy is trimmed to the natural answer length, so padding appears only in the noisy answer, and it shares the position IDs of its noisy counterpart. Visual answers. visual answer has similar structure: it starts with <BOA> <BOI>, followed by the grid of visual tokens with row separators, and ends with <EOI> <EOA>. Its tokens are denoised simultaneously rather than block by block, and no later turn conditions on it, so it needs no clean copy. generation sample therefore takes the form [ ]: the clean context followed by the noisy visual answer . At high level, noisy answer is visible only to tokens of the same answer, visual answers attend bidirectionally, and text answers follow block diffusion. The latter prevents short-response sources from dominating the mixture while contributing little to the loss. Reasoning samples use the same format in the text, image understanding, and text-to-image data. The reasoning trace is enclosed between <think> and </think> tags and followed by the final text response or image. 4.3. Multimodal Understanding Data Image understanding is the largest of the three understanding categories. Its data are drawn mainly from the public instruction-tuning collection LLaVA-OneVision (Li et al., 2025) and the private instruction data of InternVL (Wang et al., 2025a), which includes image captioning, document understanding, and chart data. To balance the mixture across skills, we organize these data by capability rather than by source dataset. This yields three capability groups: perception (image captioning, general visual question answering, grounding, and counting), text-rich image understanding (OCR, documents, charts, and GUI or web screenshots), and knowledge-intensive reasoning (science questions and mathematics). The video and 3D understanding data are limited in scale, but are constructed in the same manner as the image understanding data. The video data comprise captioning and question-answering datasets built on public video corpora, together with temporal reasoning datasets covering event ordering, counting, and temporal localization tasks (see Appendix for the full list of sources). The 3D data consist of object-centric assets paired with captions and question-answering annotations, drawn from Objaverse (Deitke et al., 2023) (with Cap3D captions (Luo et al., 2023)), GAPartNet (Geng et al., 2023), and Sketchfab (Sketchfab, 2026). 4.4. Text-to-Image Data Text-to-image generation requires training images that span broad range of concepts and domains, contain rich details, exhibit high aesthetic quality, and are accurately described by their captions. These requirements fall into three aspects: concept coverage, caption quality, and image quality. We therefore organize the construction of the text-to-image corpus into three steps, each addressing one aspect: (i) source coverage and domain-specific expansion, which broaden the range of concepts and 15 Intern Lumina U2: Multi-Codebook Diffusion Large Language Model for Omni-Visual Understanding and Image Generation domains; (ii) caption reconstruction and prompt expansion, which improve caption quality; and (iii) filtering, deduplication, and balancing, which raise image quality and reduce redundancy. Source coverage and domain-specific expansion. To cover broad range of concepts, we draw on three types of sources: (i) web-crawled imagetext pairs for the 2562 training stage; (ii) curated real-world photographs with captions in both English and Chinese; and (iii) synthetic images generated by existing text-to-image models, with the corresponding generation prompts used as captions. Nevertheless, general-purpose sources alone cannot ensure comprehensive coverage: an analysis of generated samples revealed three weak areas, namely Chinese text rendering, scientific illustrations (including physics diagrams), and text-heavy graphic designs. Rather than scaling up all sources, we construct small dedicated dataset for each weak area and upweight it individually. Caption reconstruction and prompt expansion. Because the prompt is the only conditioning signal in text-to-image generation, the quality of training prompts is critical. We construct three types of prompts: original prompts, recaptioned prompts, and reasoning-augmented prompts. Original prompts and alt-texts are retained only when they describe the image adequately. In addition, InternVL3.5-30B-A3B (Wang et al., 2025a) generates both long-form and short-form recaptioned prompt for images whose original captions are missing, mismatched, or too generic. Both recaptioned prompts describe the subjects, attributes, relations, composition, style, and visible text of the image at different descriptive granularity. During training, the prompt of each sample is randomly drawn from its original prompt and two recaptioned prompts. Finally, for subset of samples, we construct reasoning-augmented prompts by inserting reasoning trace, enclosed in <think> tags, before the target image. Within this trace, the prompt is expanded into an explicit description of the intended image. These samples are used to train the thinking mode for image generation. Filtering, deduplication, and balancing. This step consists of three stages: rule-based filtering and deduplication, model-based quality filtering, and data balancing. In the first stage, every sample must pass validity checks that require decodable image, minimum side length, and non-empty prompt with the length limit. In the second stage, every sample is scored by vision-language judge (Qwen3VL-30B-A3B-Instruct (Bai et al., 2025a)) for aesthetics, image quality, structural richness, and prompt following under the UniPercep protocol. Filtering then applies three rules in order, discarding samples with illegible or missing required text, samples below the prompt-following threshold, and samples outside the top range of aesthetic scores; the thresholds and filtering statistics are given in Appendix C. In the final stage, we balance the remaining data by adjusting the sampling multiplicity of each subset according to its content domain, language, and caption complexity. 4.5. Image Editing Data Image editing is an image-to-image (I2I) task in which the model generates target image conditioned on one or more source images with an editing instruction. valid editing sample must therefore satisfy two requirements: the target image reflects the requested change, while leaving unmentioned subjects, identities, layouts, and backgrounds unchanged. Our editing data consist of two parts: public datasets, namely OmniEdit (Wei et al., 2025), ImgEdit (Ye et al., 2025b), SEED-Data-Edit (Ge et al., 2024), X2Edit (Ma et al., 2026a), and additional in-house synthetic data. The resulting editing corpus covers ten edit types: addition, removal, replacement, adjustment, extraction, background change, style transfer, hybrid editing, action editing, and in-image text rendering. Quality control follows directly from this definition, supplemented by check on image quality. Specifically, for each sample 16 Intern Lumina U2: Multi-Codebook Diffusion Large Language Model for Omni-Visual Understanding and Image Generation we verify that (i) the target differs visibly from the source; (ii) the observed change matches the instruction; (iii) regions not referenced by the instruction remain consistent between the source and target images; and (iv) the target image is of adequate visual quality. 5. Training Strategy The Intern Lumina U2 training pipeline contains five stages that progressively increase the length of the visual context, broaden the distribution of tasks, and expand the range of supported visual modalities. At the start of training, the MoE backbone, text embedding table, and text prediction head are initialized from LLaDA2.0-mini (Bie et al., 2025). The visual embedding tables, visual input projection, and multi-codebook AR head are trained from scratch, while the AToken tokenizer remains frozen. Each stage is initialized from the preceding checkpoint, and all stages use the unified objective of Section 3.6. The same training strategy is applied on two hardware platforms: the Huawei Ascend NPU run as the primary model, while the NVIDIA GPU run as cross-platform recipe reference. 5.1. Training Stages Stage 1: VisionLanguage Alignment. Stage 1 aligns the random initialized visual modules (the visual embedding tables, visual input projection, and multi-codebook AR head) with the pretrained language backbone. The model is trained at 256 256 resolution on mixture of text-only, image captioning, and text-to-image data. Image captioning and text-to-image data provide supervision for image-to-text and text-to-image generation, respectively, while text-only data preserve the language capabilities of the backbone. Through these two complementary pathways, the model establishes an initial vision-language alignment and acquires preliminary image understanding and generation capabilities, which are further developed in the subsequent stages. Stage 2: Perception Pretraining. Stage 2 increases the training resolution to 512 512 and broadens the image understanding data to cover more demanding tasks, including OCR, grounding, document understanding, and chart understanding. The higher resolution provides the spatial detail required for fine-grained recognition and localization, particularly in text-rich documents and charts. Consequently, the model acquires fine-grained perception capabilities, which are essential for the more complex visual tasks introduced in later stages. Stage 3: Omni-Visual Mid-Training I. Stages 1 and 2 establish the basic visionlanguage alignment and the fundamental visual capabilities. The next two stages bring all visual modalities and capabilities from understanding to generation and editing into training. The first of them increases the training resolution to 1024 1024 without introducing new modalities or tasks. Empirically, we find that expanding modality coverage simultaneously with the resolution increase leads to severe degradation of previously acquired capabilities. We therefore use this stage to isolate the resolution transition: no new modalities or tasks are introduced while the model adapts its existing perception and generation capabilities to 1024 1024, allowing training to stabilize before modality coverage is expanded. Stage 4: Omni-Visual Mid-Training II. Once training at 10241024 has stabilized, the second stage of omni-visual mid-training broadens the training recipe by incorporating data for image editing, video understanding, and 3D understanding. The model learns these new tasks through the same visual interface and unified objective as in earlier stages. Image and text data from the preceding stages 17 Intern Lumina U2: Multi-Codebook Diffusion Large Language Model for Omni-Visual Understanding and Image Generation remain in the mixture so that the model retains its existing capabilities. The two stages of omni-visual mid-training share combined token budget, which amounts to 500B tokens on the Ascend run and 200B tokens on the NVIDIA run, as reported in Table 3. Stage 5: Supervised Fine-Tuning for Instruction Following. This stage fine-tunes the model at 1024 1024 on high-quality instruction-tuning dataset curated from the previous data sources and reformatted for instruction following. The dataset covers text-to-image generation, image editing, omni-visual understanding (images, videos, and 3D assets), and text-only question answering. Finetuning on these data aligns the capabilities acquired in earlier stages with instruction-following behavior, enabling the model to understand task instructions and produce the corresponding outputs. The quality-filtered data further improve the overall performance of the model. We also use lower learning rate than in previous stages, so that the model gradually adapts to the instruction-following distribution while retaining the knowledge and generation quality it has already developed. 5.2. The proportions of the data mixture for each stage are provided in Table 2. On the Ascend platform, we use 1,024 Ascend 910B NPUs in all stages; on the NVIDIA platform, we use 192 GPUs in all stages. On both platforms, the global batch size equals the number of devices, and Stages 1 and 2 process 50B and 200B tokens, respectively. In the subsequent stages, the token budgets on the Ascend platform are 500B for omni-visual mid-training (Stages 3 and 4 combined) and 300B for SFT, compared with 200B for each on the NVIDIA platform. 5.3. Optimization and Parallel Training Optimizer. We optimize the trainable 2D and 3D weight matrices, including the attention, feedforward, expert, and projection weights, with Muon (Jordan et al., 2024), which has been shown to match AdamW with substantially fewer training tokens (Liu et al., 2025a) and to remain stable on trillion-parameter MoE models (Kimi Team, 2025, 2026). For the query, key, and value projections, we use the per-head variant of Kimi K3 (Kimi Team, 2026), which orthogonalizes the update of each attention head separately. This removes only the padding inserted between samples, while retaining the padding within single sample. The data collator also records the cumulative sequence lengths of the packed samples, which mark the sample boundaries to confine attention and loss computation to each sample. Therefore, this packing strategy reduces sequence-level padding overhead while retaining sample-internal padding, without altering the objective for any individual sample. We ablate the two plateau controls of PHV (Section 6.2.2), the change threshold δp and the confidence floor fp, on 6 6 grid with 553 prompts per cell (Figure 11); the remaining controls are fixed at their default values. The two parameters act as serial gate rather than as independent controls: δp determines which positions become eligible for early commitment, and fp only limits how many of the eligible positions commit. As result, the influence of fp on the number of refinement steps increases by 17.6 from the strictest to the loosest δp, since at small δp the flatness test rarely fires and fp has little effect. The selected quality-first setting (δp=0.18, fp=0.005) lies on the speedquality frontier, reaching GenEval 89.3 at 35.9 per image. 32 Intern Lumina U2: Multi-Codebook Diffusion Large Language Model for Omni-Visual Understanding and Image Generation Figure 11: Inference-sampling ablation over the plateau change threshold δp and confidence floor fp, 553 prompts per cell. (a) GenEval over the 6 6 grid; the black box marks the selected quality-first setting δp=0.18, fp=0.005. (b) Speedquality frontier over all 36 cells, i.e. the configurations not improved on in both latency and quality by any other cell; the selected setting (red) reaches GenEval 89.3 at 35.9 per image (4.45). 8. Conclusion We have presented Intern Lumina U2, to our knowledge the first unified understanding-andgeneration diffusion language model that models multi-codebook visual states in fully discrete space and extends visual understanding across images, videos, and 3D assets. Its visual input interface preserves codebook identity by assigning each codebook an independent embedding table and merging the resulting embeddings into single backbone token through concatenation and projection. Its visual output interface uses multi-codebook AR head to predict the codes at each visual position autoregressively along the codebook dimension, while masked diffusion refines all spatial positions in parallel. Ablation studies confirm the contribution of both design choices. Codebook-specific input embeddings improve next-code top-1 accuracy, with the largest gains on later codebooks. The multi-codebook AR head captures inter-code dependencies and achieves the best results on all four generation benchmarks, with the most pronounced gains in counting, position, and attribute binding. At the system level, the primary model is trained on 1,024 Huawei Ascend 910B NPUs and provides the main reported results. reference model, trained independently on NVIDIA GPUs with the same architecture and optimization recipe but smaller training budget, is used to assess cross-platform consistency. In addition, our proposed temporal-stability-guided sampling strategy reduces image generation latency by 4.45 under the same evaluation protocol without degrading generation quality. Overall, the results on omni-visual understanding, image generation, image editing, and physically grounded scientific-diagram generation demonstrate the potential of fully discrete diffusion language modeling to unify broad visual understanding and high-quality generation within single framework. Despite these advances, several limitations remain. First, the multi-codebook autoregressive head introduces additional decoding overhead, and high-resolution generation produces long visual sequences. Second, the current system covers image generation and editing, but has not yet been extended to video or 3D generation. In future work, we plan to extend generation to videos and 3D assets, explore more tightly interleaved multimodal generation, investigate post-training with reinforcement learning, and scale up the backbone. 33 Intern Lumina U2: Multi-Codebook Diffusion Large Language Model for Omni-Visual Understanding and Image Generation

Data validation. Before training, the annotations and sequence lengths of each data mixture are precomputed offline, and sources unchanged from previous mixture are reused after their first sample is checked for consistency, while changed or new sources are processed again. The precomputed data pass four checks before use: (i) the numbers of sources and samples match the mixture definition; (ii) randomly drawn samples are non-empty and can be parsed; (iii) on random subset, recomputed sequence lengths equal the stored ones; and (iv) random subset can be converted into packed training sequences without error. Text-to-image quality filtering. As described in Section 4, the vision-language judge Qwen3-VL30B-A3B-Instruct scores every image under the UniPercep protocol on four axes, each ranging from 0 to 100: aesthetics (composition, color and lighting, and artistic expression), image quality (sharpness, artifacts, and anatomical errors), structural richness, and prompt following (subject, count, attributes, scene, style, and text requirements). Under this protocol, the judge answers each axis with twoletter code for one of four score bands (025, 2650, 5175, and 76100), which avoids its bias toward particular digits, and the continuous score is the expectation over the bands weighted by the predicted code probabilities. Filtering then applies three rules in order: images with illegible or missing required text are discarded, images with prompt-following score below 60 are discarded, and among the remaining images only those in the global top 70% by aesthetic score, threshold of about 74, are kept. Ascend Adaptation Details Intern Lumina U2 is trained, evaluated, and served entirely on Ascend NPUs. Porting the code from GPUs requires changes in three respects, since the available operators, the interface semantics of the fused kernels, and the memory capacity of each NPU all differ from those of the GPU software stack, and the following paragraphs describe how each difference is handled. Execution path. Every entry point imports torch_npu.contrib.transfer_to_npu before any model code. This remaps torch.cuda onto the NPU runtime, so no cuda literal in the model files has to be rewritten. Each rank is given its own HF_MODULES_CACHE directory; otherwise the ranks sharing node write the same dynamically imported module files at the same time. The AToken decoder 46 Intern Lumina U2: Multi-Codebook Diffusion Large Language Model for Omni-Visual Understanding and Image Generation ships with flash_attn dependency that does not exist on this platform, so its attention modules are rebuilt on the native kernels. That rebuild covers the image-decoding path; the understanding and text paths never reach that code. Fused mixture-of-experts. We rebuild the fused MoE path on torch_npu.npu_grouped_matmul, since the fused path of the GPU stack is Triton kernel. The forward pass permutes tokens into expert order with npu_moe_token_permute, then runs one grouped matrix multiplication against the merged first projection, npu_swiglu, and second grouped matrix multiplication against the second projection. The routing weights are applied as the result is unpermuted. The kernel provides no backward pass, so we write one as an explicit autograd function. It uses two further grouped matrix multiplications: one against the transposed weights for the input gradient, and one against the transposed activations, under different grouping mode, for the weight gradient. An expert-parallel variant wraps the same kernel in all-to-all dispatch and combine. Attention kernel semantics. Attention uses torch_npu.npu_fusion_attention in the BNSD layout, with the TND layout and actual_seq_qlen available for variable-length batches. Two interface details change results silently, and both are handled explicitly. First, the mask polarity is inverted relative to the SDPA convention: the kernel reads True as masked, so the additive 4D mask is converted and negated rather than passed through. Second, the variable-length interface ignores atten_mask and behaves as if no mask had been supplied, so it can express only full bidirectional attention or one template shared by every segment. The task-aware mask of Section 3.5 gives each packed segment its own pattern, so packed training uses the dense path, where the mask reaches the kernel exactly as specified. Memory. Per-NPU memory is the binding constraint of the training configuration, which makes activation allocation first-order target rather than detail absorbed by spare capacity. runs with PYTORCH_NPU_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True and The allocator MULTI_STREAM_MEMORY_REUSE=2. Three further settings determine the usable ceiling. The data-parallel shard group size is 24 or 32 depending on the size of the job, which trades parameter and optimizer residency against communication volume. Gradient checkpointing is enabled on the backbone blocks. The cache-release interval is 20 steps rather than 100, which keeps fragmentation from accumulating across the long tail of packed sequence lengths. Together they lower peak memory and raise the longest sequence one NPU can hold, which is the quantity that sets training efficiency at fixed hardware. Inference. trained checkpoint stores the 256 experts of layer as one stacked tensor. The platform provides grouped matrix-multiplication kernel, so Ascend inference loads that layout directly and serves the training-time weights unchanged. The GPU path has no such kernel: it must first split the stacked tensor into per-expert weights, which costs conversion pass and second copy of the expert parameters. E.
